processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Spring, the normal single main picking for Wuyi rock teas; little is recorded for this bush specifically.
appearance_dry: Dark brown, glossy strips, in the way of Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: A trade account gives only a high, long-lasting fragrance. Finer detail is not well recorded; expect the roast and mineral weight typical of the class.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas: water near the boil and short steeps.

vintage_note: Usually sold, as Wuyi rock teas are, by spring harvest year and roast. It is a small-volume famous-bush name, so ask for the lot's year and growing area.
description:
Lao Jun Mei is a name with two lives: a famous bush of the Wuyi Mountains, and a tea served in the novel Dream of the Red Chamber. Whether those are the same tea is an old argument.

As a Wuyi tea it is made in the way usual for the class, with shaking, partial oxidation and a roast. It sits on some lists of ten famous Wuyi bushes, though those lists differ.

The few descriptions speak of dark, glossy leaf and a high, lasting fragrance. Brew it like other rock teas: hot water, short steeps, and a little patience after the first two.

Do not confuse it with Laojunmei from Hong'an in Hubei, which carries a Chinese geographical indication under nearly the same name. Check the origin on the label.
history:
Qing-era lists of Wuyi famous bushes include Lao Jun Mei, and a modern account names it among the bushes being expanded into demonstration production. A trade article says monks of Tianxin Yongle Temple first selected it at Jiulong Ke, and that the surviving mother plant was located in 1980; treat that as a single account.

Its fame owes much to chapter 41 of Dream of the Red Chamber, where the matriarch Jia Mu refuses Liu An tea and the nun Miaoyu tells her that this is Lao Jun Mei. Commentators have read that tea as a silver-needle tea from Junshan on Dongting Lake, as this Wuyi bush, or as something else. Some recent writers favour Wuyi, but it is not settled.
